title: The Czech Benoni
description: The Czech Benoni is an easy-to-learn defense that can become your main weapon with Black against 1.d4. You simply lock up the position and launch a huge attack.

r1bqk2r/1p1nbpp1/p2p4/2pP3n/2P1P2p/2NB3P.text:
White castles. 

Let's occupy the e5-square.

r1bqk2r/1p2bp2/p2p4/2pPn1p1/2P1PN1p/2NB2.text:
And now we kick away the f4-knight. 

White's bishops are very passive. If White gets rid of our knight on g3, the h-file will be open for attack.

r1bqk2r/1p2bpp1/p2p1nn1/2pPp3/2P1P2p/2NB.text: We give ourselves the option of future line-opening with ...b5. The alternative plan of ...Nh7 and ...Bg5, playing to control the kingside dark squares, would be ineffectual since White's king hasn't castled kingside.

r1bqk2r/1p2bpp1/p2p4/2pPn2n/2P1PN1p/2NB3.text:
White wants to trade some pieces to ease the attack.

We won't make it easy for them.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbp2/3p4/2pPp1pn/2P1P2p/2NBB2.text:
...is answered with ...g5! 

Going for the dark-squared grip yet again.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pP3p/2P1PB2/2NB4.text:
White recaptures.

Let's claim a little more kingside space.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pP4/2P1PB1p/2NB3.text:
White stops our pawn from advancing.

But this has weakened g3 somewhat. Let's target the dark squares with our f6-knight.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pPp2p/2P1P3/2NB3.text:
White goes for h3, the second most popular move in this position.

We can achieve our ...h4-move.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pPp2p/2P1P3/2NB4.text:
White castles here, which occurs in 50% of the games.

Let's push even further!

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pPp2p/2P1PP2/2NB.text:
White goes for kingside activity immediately, which is a dubious plan.

We'll capture on f4 and bear in mind that e5 can be a useful square later on for our d7-knight.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P2p/2NB3.text:
White stops the h-pawn.

We slowly but surely start to get our knights onto better squares.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P2p/2NBB.text:
White develops the dark-squared bishop.

Be3 could indicate that White will castle queenside, so we won't be going for ...Nh5 and ...g5 later.

We'll bring the other knight to g6, starting with Nf8.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p4/2pP3n/2P1P2p/2NB3P/.text:
White retreats.

The bishop on h2 is eyeing the d6-pawn and combined with Nb5, it could be weak.

Hence we play the prophylactic a6, keeing the knight at bay.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p4/2pP3n/2P1PB1p/2NB3P.text:
White recaptures with the bishop.

We'll trade.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p4/2pP3n/2P1PN1p/2NB3P.text:
White recaptures with the knight.

Now we have a beautiful outpost.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p4/2pP4/2P1PN1p/2NB2nP.text:
White saves the rook.

Let's restrict White's pieces even further!

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p4/2pPp2n/2P1P2p/2NBB2.text: The third most popular move Be3...

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p4/2pPp2n/2P1P2p/P1NB3.text:
White goes for the second most popular move, a3. 

The plan is to put pressure on our queenside.

Our aim is to grab control over the kingside dark squares near the white king, so trading off the dark-squared bishops is a great plan here.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p4/2pPp2n/2P1PP1p/2NB3.text:
White creates a counterattack to not stay passive.

In the future, we want to occupy the e5-square, so a trade is in place.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2NB4/.text:
White applies the mentioned plan.

Before rerouting, it is a good idea for us to gain space on the kingside.

r1bqk2r/pp2bp2/3p4/2pPn1p1/2P1P2p/2NB2nP.text:
And Black finally occupies the e5-square.

Here, we can keep the king on e8 and enjoy a nice grip over the light-squares!

The attack could continue with ...g4, which is complemented by the bishop on c8.

r1bqk2r/pp2bpp1/3p1nn1/2pPp3/2P1P2p/2NBB.text:
White castles queenside. 

Looks like they are safe.

r1bqk2r/pp2bpp1/3p4/2pPn3/2P1PN1p/2NB3P/.text:
And we establish our strong central knight yet again. 

The plan now is to create a queenside counterplay, starting with ...a6.

Going for ...g5 and ...g4 would be a mistaken plan here. 

We shouldn't open up our king since White has the open f-file and we've traded one of our defensive knights.

r1bqk3/pp1n1pp1/3p3r/2pPp1bn/1PP1P2p/P1N.text:
Via a rook lift, Black potentially adds an attacker to the kingside.

The bishops will get traded, which plays into our hands as the f4-square will be used as an outpost.

r1bqkn1r/pp2bpp1/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P2p/2NBB.text: White sees our forces massing on the kingside and prepares to castle queenside.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2NB4/P.text:
White wants to go for the Nge2 setup, so developing the bishop to d3 is on the board.

Our b8-knight starts to reroute towards the kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/5n2/2pPp3/2P5/2N5/PP2P.text:
White develops by bringing out the knight.

We now support the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2pP4/2P5/8/PP2PPPP.text:
White expands in the center. 

Now it's time for us to strike in the center with e5.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N5/PP.text:
White expands in the center.

We continue by getting out our kingside pieces.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White controls the d5-square.

We'll challenge their center with c5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to this course about the Czech Benoni, a fighting way to play against the queen's pawn!

The Czech Benoni is an excellent way to catch your opponents off guard, get imbalanced positions, and steer things away from the typical queen's pawn structures.

Let's get to it!

1r1qk2r/1p1bbpp1/p2p1nn1/2pPp2p/P1P1P2P/.text: White is still deciding where to castle.

1rq1k2r/1p1bbpp1/p2p1nn1/2pPp2p/P1P1P2P/.text: And after ...Qc8 we control some kingside light-squares, but most importantly, we prepare a nice maneuver with ...Bd8 to ...Ba5, to control the queenside dark-squares!

r1bqk2r/1p2bpp1/p2p1nn1/2pPp2p/2P1P2P/2N.text:
White develops.

We'll support the ...b5 pawn break.

r1bqk2r/1p2bpp1/p2p1nn1/2pPp3/2P1P2p/2NB.text:
White tries to open up the kingside.

Let's prepare ...b5 even further.

r1bqk2r/pp1nBpp1/3p4/2pnp2p/2P1P3/2NB4/P.text: White's bishop is hanging, so they trade.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbp1n/3p2p1/2pPp2p/2P1P2P/2NB.text: We target the h4-pawn, which is now in trouble.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbp2/3p1np1/2pPp2p/2P1P3/2NB2.text:
White goes for castling.

Let's kick the knight from g3.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbp2/3p2p1/2pPp2n/2P1P2p/2NB4.text: And after ...Nh5 we prepare the dark-squared invasion.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pPp1Bp/2P1P3/2NB.text: White goes for the dark-squared bishop development, but this is a mistake, allowing for a nice tactic with Nxd5.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pPp2p/2P1P2P/2NB.text:
This is a very rare move, but a great choice by White!

For now, we stick to our rerouting plan.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pPp2p/2P1P3/2NB1.text:
White supports their e4-pawn, the third most popular move.

Even here, it is a good idea to continue expanding on the kingside.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pPp2p/2P1P3/2NB2.text: White immediately jumps to the g3-square, threatening to jump to the f5-square, which we can easily prevent.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbpp1/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P2p/2NBB.text:
White brings the bishop to e3.

We don't castle here. Instead, we'll reroute the knight via f8 to g6.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2NB4/.text:
White places their knight to e2.

We'll gain space on the kingside.

r1bqk2r/pp1nnpp1/3p4/2p1p2p/2P1P3/2NB4/P.text:
And we can recapture back with the knight! 

With an extra pawn this is a great position.

r1bqk2r/pp2bpp1/3p1nn1/2pPp2p/2P1P2P/2NB.text:
White covers the f4-square.

We have to be flexible here, with plans on both sides of the board.

Let's play a6.

r1bqk2r/pp2bpp1/3p1nn1/2pPp3/2P1P2p/2NBB.text:
White castles.

Ideally, we would want to prepare a queenside attack with ...b5.

r1bqkn1r/pp2bpp1/3p1n2/2pPp2p/2P1P2P/2NB.text:
White supports the e4-pawn.

Let's fight for the f4-square, as per usual.
If Ng3 to attack the pawn on h5...

r1bqkn1r/pp2bpp1/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P2p/2NBB.text:
White prepares to castle queenside.

The knight on g6 will fight for the crucial f4-square.

r1bqkn1r/pp2bpp1/3p4/2pPp2p/2P1P1nP/2NB2.text: ...Ng4 and the the pawn on h4 is lost!

r2qk2r/1p1bbpp1/p2p1nn1/2pPp2p/P1P1P2P/2.text: White stops ...b5, but we can reinforce it!

r2qk2r/1p1bbpp1/p2p1nn1/2pPp3/2P1PP1p/2N.text: White pushes, trying for kingside expansion...

r2qk2r/1p1bbpp1/p2p2n1/2pPp3/2P1PPnp/2NB.text:
...but we'll ignore the push and bring our knight to g4.

Getting rid of White's dark-squared bishop would be a great positional advantage.

In the next few moves, we'll also strive for the ...b5-push.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2NB4/P.text:
White gets the bishop out first before Nge2.

The rerouting begins with ...Nbd7 next.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2pP4/2P5/8/PP2PPPP.text:
White expands in the center.

We'll strike back with e5.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N5/PP.text:
White supports the center.

We'll develop our f8-bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White occupies the center.

We'll play to challenge it.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
For this second study, we'll explore some more continuations in the Bd3+Ne2 setup. 

These branches occur at move 8.

r1b1nrk1/pp1n1ppp/3p4/2pPp1q1/2P1P3/2N5/.text: And when White tries to trade off our active queen, we should definitely decline this trade.

r1b1nrk1/pp1nq2p/3p1pp1/2pP4/2P1PQ2/2NN4.text:
Natural is now Rf2, preparing to triple on the semi-open f-file.

Black now occupies the created e5 outpost.

r1b1nrk1/pp1nqp1p/3p2p1/2pP4/2P1PQ2/2NN4.text:
White takes back with the queen.

The threat could be e5, which would open up lines for the attack. 

Preventing it is a good idea here.

r1b1nrk1/pp1nqp1p/3p2p1/2pP4/2P1PR2/2NN4.text:
And now we play ...Qe7, activating our queen and preparing ...Ne5.

The computer evaluation lingers around equality, but the position is very imbalanced.

After ...Ne5, we can proceed with ...Bd7, ...Ng7 and ...Rae8. A timely ...f5 break is also on the cards.

r1b1nrk1/pp1nqp1p/3p2p1/2pPp3/2P1P3/2NN4.text:
And we play ...g6.

The plan is simple - we'll move our knight to g7 and advance ...f5.

r1b1nrk1/pp1nqp1p/3p2p1/2pPp3/2P1PP2/2NN.text:
The most critical and direct way for White to proceed is to advance f4.

As per usual, Black frees up the e5-square here.

r1b1nrk1/pp2q2p/3p1pp1/2pPN3/2P1PQ2/2N5/.text: And when White takes our knight, we will recapture with the d-pawn, so ...f5 is possible in the future.

r1b1nrk1/pp2q2p/5pp1/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N1Q3/P.text:
White moves their queen to safety, keeping eyes on the c5-pawn.

Let's add some support to it.

r1bq1r1k/p3bpnp/1p1p1npB/2PPp3/2P1P3/P1N.text:
White captures the c5-pawn.

We'll recapture , towards the center.

r1bq1r1k/p3bpnp/3p1npB/2pPp3/2P1P3/P1N2N.text:
White takes the open b-file.

Now Ng8 comes in handy to eject the strong h6-bishop.

r1bq1r1k/pp2bpnp/3p1npB/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N4P.text: White brings their knight back, looking to play Nd3 and push f4.

r1bq1rk1/p2nbpnp/1p1p2p1/2PPp3/2P1P3/P1N.text:
White captures the c5-pawn.

We'll recapture and bring our knight into the game.

r1bq1rk1/p2nbpnp/1p1p2pB/2pPp3/1PP1P3/P1.text:
Logical is Qd2, activating the queen and connecting the rooks.

An idea to kick away the annoying bishop on h6 is to go for ...Nf6 aimed at g4.

r1bq1rk1/p3bpnp/1p1p1npB/2pPp3/1PP1P3/P1.text:
White goes h3, preventing ...Ng4.

White has avoided ...Ng4, but we have another option of kicking away the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/p3bpnp/3p2p1/2pPp3/2P1P3/P1N2N2.text:
And we take back with the b-pawn.

White's queenside advance didn't yield much. We've got a pleasant position and will proceed with ...f5.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbpnp/3p2p1/2pPp3/1PP1P3/P1N.text:
White develops their bishop.

Now White is threatening dxc5, as ...Nxc5 can be met with Bxc5, so let's support c5 even further.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbpnp/3p2pB/2pPp3/1PP1P3/P1N.text:
White advances their b-pawn.

Let's support c5.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbpnp/3p2pB/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N2N.text:
White goes Qd2, activating their queen and connecting the rooks.

Let's use similar ideas to the previous line.
We go Ng7, with the plan of ...Nf6 and either ...Ng4 or ...Kh8 & ...Ng8.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N2N.text:
White also castles.

Our bishop on e7 could use some breathing space!

r1bq1rk1/pp2bpnp/3p1npB/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N2N.text:
White goes h3, stopping ...Ng4.

Now we free up the g8-square.

r1bq1rnk/p3b1np/3p4/2pPpp2/2P5/P1N1BN1P/.text:
We can recapture with the g-pawn. 

We are doing very well here and ...f4 is a threat to win material.

White does have control over the open b-file, but that's not relevant since there are no infiltration points.

r1bq1rnk/p3bpnp/3p2p1/2pPp3/2P1P3/P1N1BN.text:
White brings their bishop back.

Finally we can expand with f5.

r1bq1rnk/pp2bpnp/3p2pB/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N4P/.text:
And we play ...Ng8.

We've got the setup that we want and will look to proceed with ...f5.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N2N2.text:
Most often, White develops their light-squared bishop to e2.

This is played 42% of the time. 

White clearly states that they will castle kingside, without any f-pawn pushes yet, so we can castle as well.

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1p1p/3p2p1/2pP2b1/2P1PB2/2N.text:
White recaptures with the bishop.

Now we trade the bishops.

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1p1p/3p2p1/2pPp1b1/2P1P3/2N.text:
White jumps the knight into d3.

The threat is f4, so we have to go for the trade.

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1p1p/3p2p1/2pPp1b1/2P1PP2/2.text:
White advances their f-pawn.

It's important we trade on f4.

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1p1p/3p2p1/2pPp3/2P1P3/2NN4.text: And when White recaptures, we'll place our queen on a square from where it has more scope.

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1ppp/3p4/2pP2b1/2P1PB2/2N5/.text:
White recaptures with the bishop.

We continue to exchange.

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1ppp/3p4/2pPp1B1/2P1P3/2N5/.text:
White can also trade the bishops.

We recapture.

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1ppp/3p4/2pPp1b1/2P1P3/2NN4.text:
Usually, White responds by bringing their knight to d3.

We don't have to immediately trade on c1, so we make improving moves first.

r1bqnrk1/pp1n1ppp/3p4/2pPp1b1/2P1PP2/2N5.text:
White can also respond with f4.

This is played 15% of the time, and should be captured.

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbp1p/3p2p1/2pPp3/1PP1P3/P1N.text:
Most often, White follows up on their previous move with b4.

The g7-square can now be used for our knight to prepare ...f5 in the future.

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbp1p/3p2p1/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N5/.text:
White brings their knight back, looking to play Nd3 and push f4.

We'll trade off White's strong dark-squared bishop!

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbp1p/3p2pB/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N2N.text: White can also go for Bh6, but we already know how to deal with this.

White proceeds with Bh6, looking to exploit the weakened dark-squares and attacking our rook

The only way to save the rook is to block.

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbp1p/3p2pB/2pPp3/2P1P3/P1N2.text:
The idea is to try to exploit our weakened dark-squares.

We have to block the attack.

This is played 33% of the time.

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbppp/3p4/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N1BN2.text:
White's third option is to simply develop the dark-squared bishop.

This is played 10% of the time.

We'll play g6, again planning the ...Ng7 and ...f5 expansion.

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbppp/3p4/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N2N2/.text:
White's final option is Rb1, with the idea to support a b-pawn advance.

This is only played about 5% of the time, but still worth analyzing.

Here, the g7-square will be used as a rerouting square as well.

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbppp/3p4/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N5/PP.text:
Their idea is to play Nd3 and f4 before we can advance ...f5.

Our dark-squared bishop isn't complementary to our structure, so we'll trade it off.

r1bqnrk1/pp1nbppp/3p4/2pPp3/2P1P3/P1N2N2.text:
White's second option is a3, preparing to push the b-pawn.

This is played 20% of the time.

We'll prepare a future ...f5.

r1bqnrk1/pp3ppp/3p4/2pPn3/2P1PR2/2N5/PP2.text:
And we jump our knight into e5.

One major downside for White here is that there's no convenient way to challenge or trade off our knight. Nd3 loses the c4-pawn, and Nf3 loses the exchange to ...Ng6.

Our plan is to proceed with ...Qe7, ...Bd7, and to try to advance on the queenside with our a and b pawns.

r3nrk1/p2bq2p/1p3pp1/2pPp3/2P1P2P/2N1Q3/.text: And if White tries to launch a kingside attack, as seen in the game Nielsen - Carlsen, 2007...

r4rk1/p2bq2p/1p1n1pp1/2pPp3/2P1P2P/2N1Q3.text:
We can simply go ...Nd6.

Magnus went on to win the game.

A strong plan is to double rooks and advance the f-pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N2N2/.text:
And White develops their knight.

This move will be the focus of this chapter. White develops the knight to the most active square, but in turn, blocks their f-pawn.

Yet again, Black goes for the rerouting of the queen's knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/5n2/2pPp3/2P5/2N5/PP2P.text:
White develops their queenside knight, preparing to advance e4.

We'll strengthen our center with d6.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2pP4/2P5/8/PP2PPPP.text:
White responds by advancing their d-pawn, taking even more space.

Now we'll push in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N5/PP.text:
White advances their e-pawn.

We'll develop our king's bishop and prepare to castle.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White advances their c-pawn, taking more space in the center.

We'll challenge their central control by playing c5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
For this chapter, we will be seeing more setups that are also high in popularity. 

We'll examine the very natural Nf3+Be2 or Bd3 setups.

lessons.title: Other Bishop Moves - Bd3 and Bg5

r1b2rk1/pp1nqppp/3p4/2pPN2n/2P1P3/2N5/PP.text:
White can also go for tactics by capturing the e5-pawn.

This, however, isn't a good idea.

We capture with our knight.

r1b2rk1/pp1nqppp/3p4/2pPp2n/2P1P3/2N2N2/.text:
Most often, White castles.

Now, the f4-square is free.

r1b2rk1/pp1nqppp/3p4/2pPp3/2P1Pn2/2N2NP1.text:
White goes g3, looking to remove our knight from the f4-square.

Retreating it would be too passive.

r1b2rk1/pp2q1pp/3p4/2pPn2B/2P1Pp2/2N5/PP.text:
And now we advance ...f4.

rnb1k2r/1p1p1ppp/4pq2/pPb5/2P1n3/4PN2/P4.text: ...but after ...Qf6 the rook on a1 is trapped!

rnb2rk1/pp1p1ppp/1q2pn2/2b3B1/2P5/2N1PN2.text:
White blocks.

But we can still capture on b2.

rnb2rk1/pp1p1ppp/4pB2/2b5/2P5/2N1PN2/Pq3.text: White captures our knight, intending to damage our pawn structure.

rnb2rk1/pp1p1ppp/4pB2/8/1bP5/2N1PN2/Pq3P.text:
But instead of recapturing, we add an attacker to the knight! 

White's king doesn't feel safe.

rnb2rk1/pp1p1ppp/4pq2/2b5/2PNP3/2N1K3/PP.text: The king defends the knight, but now we simply add an attacker.

rnbq1rk1/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2b5/2PNP1n1/2N5/PP.text:
White blocks the attack by jumping to d4.

Seems like they have covered the attack successfully, but Black has a tactical shot.

rnbq1rk1/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2b5/2PNP3/2N5/PP3K.text:
White recaptures.

Now we can fork the king and knight.

rnbq1rk1/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2b3B1/2P5/2N2N2/P.text:
White pins our knight.

We'll unpin with Qb6, when we hit both f2 and b2!

rnbq1rk1/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2b5/2P1P3/2N2N2/P.text:
White continues with the third most popular move, which is e4, immediately gaining space in the center.

As e3 wasn't pushed, we can continue by attacking f2.

rnbq1rk1/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2b5/2P5/2N1PN2/PP.text:
White blocks our bishop on c5.

We'll continue by fighting for the center.

rnbq1rk1/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2b5/2P5/2N2N2/PP2.text: And after ...O-O we transpose to the main line.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2bP4/8/2N1PN2/PP3PP.text:
White trades.

We'll take back with the pawn.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/5n2/2bp4/8/2N1PN2/PP2BPP.text:
White prepares to castle.

We'll continue our development, starting with the knight.

rnbqk2r/1p1p1ppp/4pn2/pPb5/2P5/5N2/P3PPP.text:
White develops the knight.

With the bishop on c5, we can start attacking.

rnbqk2r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2b5/2P5/2N2N2/PP2P.text:
White develops the queenside knight.

And we get our king to safety.

rnbqkb1r/1p1p1ppp/4pn2/p1P5/1PP5/8/P2BPP.text:
White defends the pawn with the bishop.

We'll simply take on b4. White's queenside pawns are shattered.

rnbqkb1r/1p1p1ppp/4pn2/pPP5/2P5/8/P3PPPP.text: White pushes even further, gaining space, but now the c5-pawn can be freely captured.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2P5/1PP5/8/P3PPPP.text:
White plays b4, trying to defend the pawn on c5.

This is the least popular move out of the three.

Our idea is to disrupt White's pawns on the queenside.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2P5/2P5/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White goes for 4.Nc3, the most popular move played in more than half of the games.

We can just recapture on c5 and get our bishop out in the meantime.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2P5/2P5/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White develops with the second most popular move, played in 20% of the games.

We can safely grab the pawn now.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2P5/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/.text:
On the third move, White grabs the c5-pawn. 

This happens very rarely, but White might try to hold onto the pawn after we continue with e6.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White gains more space.

We reply with the Benoni.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the fourth study on third-move deviations!

It is the least common move, but your opponent might grab the seemingly free pawn on c5!

r1bq1rk1/p2nppbp/1p3np1/2pp4/3PP3/2PB1N2.text:
White pushes e4 now.

Let's learn how to fight against this. We'll start by taking on d4 and reducing the sturdiness of their center.

r1bq1rk1/p2nppbp/1p3np1/3p4/3PP3/3B1N2/P.text: Once White recaptures, we'll trade yet again.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nppbp/5np1/2pp4/3P4/2PBPN2/P.text:
White slides the rook to e1 and prepares to push e4.

That's going to be their front of attack. 

Now it's time to take care of the light-squared bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npp1p/5np1/2pp4/3P4/2PBPN2/P.text:
The knight gets out to d2.

Let's plant the bishop on g7.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/5n2/2pp4/3P4/2PBPN2/PP.text:
White activates their bishop to d3.

It's a London-like structure, except their bishop is stuck on c1.

We won't go for ..e6, as this would run into the same problem of restricting the queen's bishop. Instead, we'll prepare to fianchetto the f8-bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P4/1P3N2/PBP.text:
White gets their bishop to b2, as planned.

However, it's only staring at the d4-pawn now!

Our bishop comes to g4, pinning the f3-knight.

r2q1rk1/3n1ppp/3bpn2/1Ppp4/P7/4PN2/1B3PP.text: The bishop comes out to b2 now.

r2q1rk1/pb1nppbp/1p3np1/8/3PN3/3B1N2/PP3.text:
And suddenly our bishop is extremely strong on b7.

This is an IQP position, so you should look to control the d5-square as much as possible in the near future.

You might even be able to capture on d4 at some point.

r2q1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P2b1/1P3N2/P.text:
And we'll castle.

From here on, you might face Ne5, after which you should trade on e2.

If not, beware of c4 possibilities for White at any point.

In that case, even capturing on c4 and playing on the queenside with ...Rc8 is good.

r2qk2r/3n1ppp/1pP1pn2/3p4/1b6/4PN2/P2B1P.text:
White blocks with the bishop.

We'll exchange bishops.

r2qk2r/3n1ppp/1pP1pn2/3p4/8/4PN2/P2N1PPP.text:
The knight recaptures.

Now our knight is still under attack, so we move it forward, pointing aggressively at the e4-square.

r2qk2r/3n1ppp/3bpn2/1Ppp4/P7/4PN2/5PPP/R.text:
White castles.

We'll castle as well.

r2qk2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P2b1/1P3N2/PB.text:
The d2-square is better for White's knight.

They keep their c-pawn options open.

r2qkb1r/3n1ppp/1p2pn2/2Pp4/PP6/4PN2/5PPP.text:
White could accept that they can no longer maintain the pawns and instead play to expand on the queenside.

We'll recover our pawn.

r2qkb1r/3n1ppp/1pP1pn2/3p4/1P6/4PN2/P4PP.text:
One of the options is to push the pawn and attack our knight.

But remember - that pawn was pinned to the b4-pawn!

Capturing is with check!

r2qkb1r/3n1ppp/4pn2/1Ppp4/P7/4PN2/5PPP/R.text:
They push b5 and get two connected passed pawns.

This is definitely a sound plan.

We'll develop our final minor piece and prepare to castle.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P2b1/1P3N2/PB.text:
White unpins and prepares castling.

We'll prepare to get our last minor piece out.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P2b1/1P3N2/PB.text:
White castles.

And we'll get our bishop out in readiness for castling.

r3k2r/2q2ppp/1pP1pn2/2np4/8/4PN2/P2N1PPP.text:
You can comfortably place the queen on c7 and capture the pawn next.

In the center, the e5-square is free and you should definitely push to grab more space.

White capturing on c5 has backfired in this instance; Black is much better, if not winning.

r4rk1/2qn1ppp/3bpn2/1Ppp4/P7/4PN2/1B3PPP.text:
And a good developing move for the queen is ...Qc7.

We've got a passed pawn of our own on the c-file and we should look to push it.

In the center, ...e5 is great.

Just be careful not to trade too many pieces, as then White's queenside pawns can become too strong to stop.

rn1qkb1r/3B1ppp/1p2pn2/2Pp4/1P6/4PN2/P4P.text:
White trades. 

We'll recapture with the b8-knight, adding further pressure to the pawns.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/4pn2/2Pp4/1P6/4PN2/P4PPP.text: Once White takes, we're not done chipping away at their structure on the queenside.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/4pn2/p1Pp4/1P6/2P1PN2/P4.text:
It's horrible for White to capture, of course.

So they defend the pawn with c3.

We'll take on b4, and keep trying to dismantle the white queenside pawns.

rnbqkb1r/5ppp/1p2pn2/1BPp4/1P6/4PN2/P4PP.text:
White gives a check first.

We can simply block the check.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/3P4/4PN2/PPP2P.text:
White supports the center with the pawn, but this locks their bishop on c1, and we can simply grab some space in the center.

This move is played 20% of the time, amounting to 700,000 games.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP3PP.text:
And I recommend ...g6 here, looking to play ...Bg7.

This position actually resembles the Panov Caro-Kann.

If White captures on d5, even a maneuver like ...Nbd7-Nb6 to slowly get it back is fine.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2Pp4/8/4PN2/PPP2PPP.text:
White capturing on c5 is played 13% of the time here.

White wants to take the free pawn and try to hold on to it.

We'll play e6, and if White doesn't defend the c5-pawn, we're simply going to activate our bishop on that square.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/2PP4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
The move c4 is played 18% of the time in this position.

White creates a lot of tension in the center and we have an important decision to make.

We'll capture on d4.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P4/1P2PN2/P1P.text:
Pushing b3 is played only 9% of the time, but has a logical basis  behind it.

White wants to deal with the problematic dark-squared bishop by placing it on b2.

We'll take on d4.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P4/2P1PN2/PP3.text:
The most popular move in this position is 4.c3, and it's played 23% of the time.

White solidifies the center with two pawns.

We'll bring our queen's knight out.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/1P3N2/P1P2P.text:
White recaptures with the pawn.

Usually, this would open up their dark-squared bishop, but White has already committed to the fianchetto in this line.

We should continue to develop, so we'll play Nc6.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2Pp4/1P6/4PN2/P1P2P.text:
As mentioned, expect to see b4 here a lot.

However, this way of playing lets us expand while undermining White's structure.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
Already a deviation from what we've seen before.

White activates the knight to f3 instead of playing c4.

This is designed to throw us off our game and lead to different 1.d4 positions, but we'll keep playing in Benoni style.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In the last chapter of our Czech-Benoni course, we'll take a look at the Anti-Czech Benoni, which is characterized by 2.Nf3 by White.

Some of the positions we cover in this chapter will be similar to usual Benoni structures, while others will not, which is why it's important to know.

The first study will deal with 3.e3.

3q1rk1/1p1nppbp/R2p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2N2N1P/.text: White takes on a6, and naturally we recapture.

3q1rk1/3nppbp/p2p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2N2N1P/1P.text: White might go after that pawn on a6, but we've got a nice active move to defend it.

5rk1/3nppbp/p2p1np1/q1pP4/4P3/2N2N1P/1PP.text:
And that's bringing the queen to a5.

As mentioned, we've got a bunch of space and potential on the queenside.

We'll use it by bringing the knight from f6 all the way to b5 and trying to trade it for White's knight on c3, which would connect our pawns again.

The rook can slide to b8.

r1bq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2np1n2/2p1p3/2P1P3/2N2N.text:
And we'll play ...e5.

We give up the d5-square but get a clamp on the d4-square.

This square trade-off in the center is usually fine for either side.

We'll shove our knight into d4 and White will probably jump to d5.

r1bqk2r/pp1nbppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P1P3/2N2N2.text:
And we'll get our knight out to d7.

A familiar position.

r1bqk2r/pp2b1pp/2nppn2/2p5/2P1P3/2N2N2/P.text:
The bishop comes out to e2 now.

Time to castle.

r2q1rk1/1p1nppbp/P2p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2N2N1P.text:
White captures...

And we will take back with the rook.

r2q1rk1/1p1nppbp/p2p1np1/2pP4/P3P3/2N2N2.text:
White stops it with a4.

But at the very least we now know where we should focus our play on.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1pb1/3p1npp/2pP4/7B/2NB1Q1P/.text:
And we'll develop the knight, eyeing that e5-square.

The trade on f3 came in handy after already having traded the pawns on d5.

Now the position is somewhat more comfortable to play for us.

r2q1rk1/pp1nppbp/3p1np1/1PpP4/4P3/2N2N1P.text:
White goes for h3, which is potentially useful to keep our knight out of g4.

We'll challenge on the queenside.

r2q1rk1/pp1nppbp/3p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2N2N2/P.text:
The rook slides to e1 to support the center.

The center is closed, our king is on the kingside, but we've got a lot of space on the queenside, and we'll prepare to expand with a later ...b5.

r2qk2r/pp1nppbp/3p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
White castles.

We'll get our king into safety as well.

r2qnrk1/1p1nppbp/p2p2p1/2pP4/P3P3/2N2N2/.text:
That's why ...Ne8 is logical.

We'll reroute the knight to c7 and slide the rook to b8.

After that, White won't be able to stop ...b5!

Once we achieve that push, we'll be extremely strong on the queenside.

rn1q1rk1/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/1BpP4/P3P3/2N2N.text:
They might do the same.

Now, we should evaluate whether a trade on b5 is good for us or not.

If we trade, sure, White will have a strong pawn on b5, but that pawn will also be over-extended.

We'll then be able to undermine it with ...a6 and grab a lot of space on the queenside.

rn1q1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/1PpP4/4P3/2N2N2/.text:
White recaptures with the pawn.

We continue to develop.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pb1/3p1npp/2pP4/6bB/2NB1N1P/.text: White attacks our bishop, and we'll capture on f3 in preparation for bringing a knight to e5.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pbp/3pbnp1/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPP.text:
We'll recapture with the bishop and this suddenly brings life to our position. 

We'll activate the knight and play for ...d5.

It's not the best for White to take on e6.

rn1qk2r/pp1Bppbp/3p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2N2N2/P.text:
A trade is definitely logical.

This does kind of solve White's light-squared bishop problems, but our bishop wasn't exactly active either.

rn1qk2r/pp1bppbp/3p1np1/1BpP4/P3P3/2N2N2.text:
White could choose to protect the bishop instead of trading.

The idea is that they want a pawn on b5 to prevent our future queenside expansion.

We'll castle.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2N2N2/P.text:
And so will they.

A common motif in this study is undermining White's central structure with ...e6.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2NB1N2/.text:
White does the same.

We could get the light-squared bishop out to g4 before we play ...e6, but there's not much merit to trading on f3 now, so instead we'll first play to undermine the white center.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pb1/3p1npp/2pP4/7B/2NB1N2/PP.text:
White recaptures with the pawn.

Don't be afraid if they recapture on d5 with the knight.

Your knight on f6 is safe as you can always play ...g5.

Now we'll pin the f3-knight.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pb1/3p3p/2pP2pn/8/2N2NB1/PPP.text:
And now we'll go after the bishop.

This was the point of playing ...g5, as we'll capture that active bishop now.

Meanwhile, our bishop on g7 is standing as strong as ever.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pb1/3ppn1p/2pP2p1/4P3/2N2NB1.text:
The g3-square is the only possible one to retreat to.

Now we'll capture on d5.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pb1/3ppnpp/2pP4/4P2B/2N2N2/P.text:
White retreats to h4, maintaining the pin.

We'll finally break the pin by playing g5.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pb1/3ppnpp/2pP4/4P2B/2NB1N2/.text: It will probably move to h4, after which we can continue with our central plan and capture on d5.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/3pPnp1/2p5/4P3/2N2N2/PPP.text: If White takes in any way...

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/3ppnp1/2pP2B1/4P3/2N2N2/.text:
A move like Bg5 is definitely sensible, pinning our knight.

We challenge the bishop by playing h6.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/3ppnp1/2pP2B1/4P3/2NB1N2.text:
White activates their bishop to g5 now, pinning our knight.

They don't want to capture on e6.

We'll challenge the bishop.

rnbqk2r/pp2b1pp/3ppn2/2p5/2P1P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
Expect to see e4 from White a lot.

They should gain space when they can.

We'll fight for the center ourselves.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/1BpP4/4P3/2N2N2/P.text:
The most popular choice is the active check on b5, which is played 20% of the time.

We'll just block with the bishop, as the knight will be useful later.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
The passive-looking 6.Be2 is played just under 20% of the time here.

White wants to castle.

We'll get our king into safety.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2NB1N2/P.text:
White players activate the bishop to d3 about 15% of the time.

It's definitely unorthodox to activate the bishop like this, staring at its own pawn.

We'll castle.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2pP4/8/5N2/PPP1PPP.text:
White pushes d5 and grabs space.

This prevents ...d5 from us in the future.

This move is played 17% of the time.

We'll reply with d6. This ensures that White cannot later overrun our position with e4-e5.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/3p1np1/2pP4/4P3/2N2N2/P.text:
White continues in an active manner with e4.

Let's continue our plan.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2pP4/2P5/5N2/PP2P.text:
If White plays c4 here, the position will most likely transpose to a chapter we've already covered.

That's why this move is played 61% of the time.

We'll return to our main idea of playing e5 and forming a strong mass of central pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2pP4/8/2N2N2/PPP1.text:
White developing the knight to c3 is the second most popular move here, played about 20% of the time.

To develop the dark-squared bishop, we'll opt for the fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3p1n2/2pPp3/2P5/2N2N2/PP.text:
White might choose not to capture en passant but rather develop the knight to c3.

Let's continue playing standard Benoni moves.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/3pPn2/2p5/2P5/5N2/PP2PPP.text: White can capture en passant and we don't have the option of recapturing with the d-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/3ppn2/2p5/2P5/2N2N2/PP2PP.text:
White activates the knight to c3 now.

We continue our development.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
White develops to f3 instead of playing c4 first.

We'll strike at the white center with c5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In the second study of the Anti-Czech Benoni chapter, we'll take a look at White playing d5 on move 3.

This approach resembles our known Benoni more than the first study, with some differences that we'll analyze.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/1pn2n2/3p4/2pP1B2/2P1PN.text:
And now the knight comes to d2.

Not much else White can do.

The doubled b-pawns are an asset rather than a weakness. We'll push forward with b5, targeting the white pawn chain.

r1b1kb1r/1p2pppp/2n2n2/1p1p4/2pP1B2/2P1P.text: White develops the bishop to e2.

r1b1kb1r/1p3ppp/2n1pn2/1p1p4/2pP1B2/2P1P.text:
To play ...b4, we first have to prepare it.

And a move like ...e6 is a great way to do so, as our bishop now supports the square as well.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pp1p/1qn2np1/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1P.text:
I recommend going for ...g6.

This will allow for our dark-squared bishop to attack the center from g7.

The other benefit of this move is that the g-pawn supports the f5-square for the bishop to develop to and target the queen.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1Qn2n2/3p4/2pP1B2/2P1PN.text:
Be prepared for White to capture your queen at any point.

We recapture, opening the a-file for our rook.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/1QP1P.text:
White opens up the light-squared bishop.

A great way to gain space on the queenside without creating any weaknesses is to play c4.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P1PN.text: In this instance, when White defends the center with e3...

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p4/2pP1B2/2P1PN.text:
White could choose to retreat here, but this gives us the upper hand.

It's like them admitting their mistake.

We've got a tactic here.

r1b1kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p4/3P1B2/1P2PN2.text: The d-pawn is easily protected with e3, but we have nothing to worry about in this position.

r3k2r/pp2ppb1/1qn4p/3p1bp1/2pP4/2P1PNP1/.text:
But the simple fianchetto is sufficient defense here.

Black is much better because of the clear advantage in activity.

r3kb1r/pp2pp2/1qn4p/3p1bp1/2pP4/2P1PNP1/.text:
The h-pawn recaptures, and remember to be careful here if you reach this position.

White is threatening to capture the g5-pawn, as its defender is pinned to the rook.

r3kb1r/pp2pp2/1qn4p/3p1bpn/2pP4/2P1PNB1/.text:
It has to retreat to g3 now.

It's a strong bishop. Getting rid of it is only logical.

r3kb1r/pp2ppp1/1qn4p/3p1b1n/2pP3B/2P1PN2.text:
White retreats to h4.

We can push even further!

r3kb1r/pp2ppp1/1qn4p/3p1b2/2pP4/2P1PNP1/.text: White finally develops the knight, but it doesn't have much potential.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/2pp1b2/3P1B2/2P1PN.text:
We'll activate the bishop as well.

Next, we'll look to play ...e6 and bring the rook to the c-file where White's queen is located.

Once the queenside is fully developed, we can focus on the kingside.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p1Q2/2pP1B2/2P1PN.text: If White takes it, we're winning.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p1b2/2pP1B2/2P1PN.text:
A more sensible move by White is retreating to c1.

But now their queen is extremely passive.

Let's go after their active piece.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn2n2/3p1b2/3P1B2/1P2PN2.text:
We'll bring the bishop to f5 and the upcoming moves seem natural.

We want to centralize the knight on the e4-square and open up the dark-squared bishop with ...e6.

White's b3-move has weakened the dark squares, so our dark-squared bishop could be a monster.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn5/3p1b1n/2pP4/2P1PNB1/.text: If White chooses to retreat right away, we can just take that bishop.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn5/3p1b2/2pP4/2P1PNP1/P.text:
The h-pawn recaptures.

And now we cover the h-file.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/1qn5/3p1bBn/2pP4/2P1PN2/P.text:
They can choose to slide to g5 here.

However, that just gives us more tempi.

r3kb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p1Q2/2pP1B2/2P1PN2.text:
We'll simply capture on b2 and they can't save the rook.

White can try being tricky with 9.Be2, the idea being 9...Qxa1 10.Qc2 and our queen is in trouble, but the insertion of the equally crafty 9...g6 (or e6) means their queen can't get back to c2 in order to corral ours!

r3kb1r/pp3pp1/1qn1p2p/3p1b2/2pP4/2P1PNP1.text:
And we'll simply continue with ...e6.

Now Nh4 isn't effective anymore.

White's pieces are completely cramped together with little to no prospects of immediate improvement.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1q3n2/2pp4/3P1B2/1PP2N2.text:
A way to save the pawn is certainly to push it, and White players do this 14% of the time.

The downside of this move is that it weakens White's queenside structure.

We'll take on d4, creating a slight weakness for White on b4.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1q3n2/2pp4/3P1B2/1QP2N2.text:
The most confrontational move played 47% of the time is Qb3.

White doesn't want to allow easy targets and offers a trade of queens.

We'll ignore this trade and opt for developing moves instead.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1q3n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P2N2/.text:
The move Qc1 is played only 8% of the time, and it seems really passive.

White does defend the pawn but allows for easy development by us.

You'll face Qc2 22% of the time here, and it does look logical.

White activates the queen and protects the pawn in a non-confrontational manner.

We'll develop and put pressure on d4.

rnb1kb1r/pp2pppp/1q3n2/3p4/3P1B2/1P3N2/P.text:
Once White recaptures...

We'll develop our queenside pieces.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/3P4/2P2N2/PP2P.text:
And the move 3.c3 is played 16% of the time here, or in almost      
580,000 games.

This does restrict the development of the b-knight, however.

Black can fight for the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/2pp4/3P1B2/2P2N2/PP.text:
This is the perk of 3.c3. White gets to activate the dark-squared bishop to f4.

On the other hand, a lot of the times when the bishop is activated like this, it leaves the b2-pawn undefended.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
White develops to f3 now.

We challenge the white d-pawn with c5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In the third study of this chapter, we'll take a look at the 3.c3 variation by White.

There is definitely merit to playing like this as it is logical to support the center with a pawn.

r1bqkb1r/1p1p1ppp/2n1pn2/2P5/1P6/1Q3N2/P.text: They can defend with the queen.

r1bqkb1r/3p1ppp/1pn1pn2/2P5/1P6/1Q3N2/P3.text:
In which case we can continue to chip away at that structure even further.

White is hardly going to be able to hold everything together.

rnb1k2r/pp1p1ppp/1q2pn2/2b3B1/8/2N2N2/PP.text:
We can bring the queen out and fork the two pawns on f2 and b2.

White will lose one of them and will probably have to defend for the rest of the game.

rnb1kb1r/pp1p1ppp/5n2/q3B3/3N4/8/PPP1PPP.text:
But there's another fork, and we'll win a piece.

This is what you get when you don't stick to known theory!

rnbqk2r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2b3B1/8/2N2N2/PPP1.text: If they develop the bishop, for example, thinking it's a natural developing move, there's already trouble.

rnbqkb1r/1p1p1ppp/4pn2/2P5/1P6/5N2/P3PPP.text:
White recaptures.

We'll develop with tempo, hitting b4.

rnbqkb1r/1p1p1ppp/4pn2/p1P5/1P6/2P2N2/P3.text:
White defends with c3, but they're not out of the woods yet.

We take on b4.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2P5/1P6/5N2/P1P1P.text:
If they do protect the pawn, you've probably seen this common motif in many different openings.

a5 starts to undermine the pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2P5/8/2N2N2/PPP1P.text: If they just continue developing, we'll recapture the pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2P5/8/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
White capturing the pawn certainly seems dubious, as they abandon the center.

This move is still played 9% of the time, in just under 350,000 games.

We'll open up our dark-squared bishop with the intention of recapturing the pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/3P1B2/5N2/PPP1.text:
Developing the bishop to f4 can prove to be extremely dangerous if White doesn't know what they're doing.

It's played 9% of the time.

We'll take on d4, and set a little trap.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/8/3N1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
If White recaptures with the knight, they are already lost.

We have a pawn fork!

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P4/5N2/PPP1PPPP.text:
The knight comes out to f3.

We'll play the signature Benoni move of c5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In the last study, we'll look at the two remaining options for White one move 3: 3.dxc5 and 3.Bf4.

Both of these moves are rare compared to others, and for a reason.

White abstains from logical play in an attempt to spice up the position. It often backfires.
